SKY HUSTLERS

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Pigeon racing isn’t a quirky side hustle - it’s a multimillion-rand obsession.
• A single bird can sell for R5 million.
• President Cyril Ramaphosa hosts the AfrikaPro Million Dollar Race on his Phala Phala estate.
• Foreign syndicates bet millions.
• And now? Township kids are clocking in faster birds than the elite - with none of the pedigree.

But here’s the rub:
Only a handful of South Africa’s 4,000 licensed fanciers are Black.
Most clubs remain white-owned, white-run, and white-sanctioned.
This isn’t a story about pigeons.
It’s a story about power, access, and how legacy gets built - or stolen.
While the elite race for prestige and profit, Black fanciers in the townships are often locked out - despite breeding birds that can fly just as far, just as fast.
But a shift is in the air.

And it smells like feathers and revolution.


Summary:
It’s the most unlikely battlefield for race, class, and legacy in South Africa.
Not Parliament. Not a protest.
A pigeon coop.

South Africa’s newest turf war is happening in the sky.
In battered backyards and township rooftops, a new generation of Black pigeon fanciers is taking flight - and taking on an old guard that never saw them coming.
Pigeon racing was once the playground of white suburban men: pedigree birds, pristine coops, and prize pots big enough to make a banker blush.
Now?
The game’s changing.
They’re breeding champions in shacks. Clocking birds in car boots. Raising syndicates on social grants and second chances.
And they’re not just racing pigeons -
they’re upending a bloodline sport built on exclusion… one wingbeat at a time.

Young, Black, and from the townships, they’re training world-class racers from the scrap heaps of apartheid’s leftovers.
They don’t come from money.
But they’ve got the hustle, the feathers, and the fire.
And they’re not just racing pigeons - they’re rewriting the pecking order.

Press Release:


It’s an unlikely battlefield for power, prestige and profit: not Parliament, not a protest, but a pigeon coop. Pigeon racing isn’t a quirky side hustle – it’s a multimillion-rand obsession. And traditionally, it’s the playground of the elite. But from backyards and car boots, a new generation of champions is rising as township kids breed winning birds – with none of the pedigree. They’re raising syndicates on sponsorships, upending a bloodline sport and getting ready to take on an old guard that never saw them coming. It’s a story about how legacy is built – or stolen. The story of a turf war, in the sky.
Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Govan Whittles

Script:


SKY HUSTLERS - FINAL:

(Lodumo Nkala): “One morning I was just sitting on the stoep, it was school holidays, and a cloud just flew over me. I know now that time it was 150 pigeons, that were circling, being trained, and it was the guy next door.
(GOVAN): As a seven-year-old, Lodumo Nkala remembers seeing the sky filled with birds.
(Lodumo Nkala): And I mean, that was about 15 years ago, it was actually 2010.”
(GOVAN): It was in that moment that pigeons became his passion.
(Lodumo Nkala): “Life is up and down at times, but one thing that has remained is pigeons - no matter where I’ve been.”
(GOVAN): At 22, Lodumo is trying to break into a sport with a reputation for attracting competitors with deep pockets.
(Lodumo Nkala): “It’s been a long journey, a difficult one… this is all part of the hard work, so it’s slowly showing.”
(GOVAN): A boyhood passion has become a fight for space in pigeon racing.

(Lodumo Nkala): “When I started pigeons I was a lot younger. Scared, confused, lost, not a lot of information. But I had a burning passion; everyday was just pigeons, pigeons, pigeons, so ya, it was tough, it was really tough man.”
(GOVAN): Not yet competing, he’s come a long way and is building a reputation as what’s known as a “fancier”.
(Govan): “Tell me what a fancier is.”
(Lodumo Nkala): “A pigeon fancier is someone who, who, who rears pigeons, who’s a breeder, they train pigeons, they fly. Whether you’re racing or not, you are considered a pigeon fancier.”

(GOVAN): Now, he’s in the townships, making an elite sport truly accessible.
(Lodumo Nkala): “I started ‘Community Lofts’ - which is basically an organisation introducing pigeon racing to South African townships. It hosts pigeon events, training programmes, education. And at Community Lofts we are able to provide mentorship to fanciers who, who are looking to get into the sport.”

(GOVAN): And this is all happening while breeding what he hopes will be race-winners.

(Govan) 'So, you designed this yourself, yeah’
(Lodumo Nkala) “Ya, no. So what you see here is a breeding station, an open loft breeding station - meaning the pigeons will all be mixed in here, and then breed from here. So.”
(Govan) ‘This is like a singles club.’
(Lodumo Nkala): “Exactly! Ya, choose, choose who you want, so that’s the aim of this. Because look, pigeons have the ability to, to choose champions themselves, so…”
(Govan) ‘Hey Chief! Okay.’

(Govan): Pigeon racing is a global sport worth billions of Rands, with some birds selling for small fortunes. The highest ever price paid for a top racing pigeon was more than 30 million Rands.
(Govan): Even President Cyril Ramaphosa hosts a race, drawing entries from around the world.

FTB

(NATSOUND) “We’re racing about 60 birds tonight…”
(Lodumo Nkala) “Nice!”

(GOVAN): The Benoni Homing Society on Joburg’s East Rand is a far less extravagant setting, but it has a proud 120-year racing history.
(GOVAN): Race days start with birds being scanned, sealed in crates, and sent hundreds of kilometres away.
(GOVAN): Released together, they race home with tiny chips on their legs.
(GOVAN): Sensors clock the moment they land, and the fastest average speed wins.
(GOVAN): Lodumo is here to learn, but he’s not yet a member.
(GOVAN): Tonight, this truck is carrying someone else’s team, but Lodumo is hoping it’ll be one of his own next season.

(Lodumo Nkala) “We’re trying to establish our own club. It’s got its own challenges, but soon we can, we can hopefully get something like this going.”

(GOVAN): Lodumo uses Community Lofts to pass on what he’s learning, and he’s taken 74-year-old, Glenn Masekwane under his wing.
(Glenn Masekwane): “This is our starter pack.”
(Govan): “This is the beginning of the home of champions.”
(Glenn Masekwane): “Yeah. ‘Casa du Champione’, in Portuguese.”

(GOVAN): Glenn’s own passion for pigeons was ignited in a moment of grief.
(Glenn Nasekwane): “My nephew was brutally killed in Maboneng, and at his funeral there was a release of these white, you know, pigeons… But it was until I met Lodumo… he just opened my eyes into this hidden, you know, sport with great potential.”

(Govan): “How did you find the pigeon racing community in South Africa?”
(Glenn Masekwane): “It is a rich man’s sport. Yeah, it’s like horse racing, the elite of the elite. But surprise surprise, there are people like myself, we really are getting into this - it’s an industry.”

(GOVAN): Glenn believes the sport still shuts out people without money and needs to transform.

GOVAN LINK: “It’s not Parliament or protest. But in its own way, pigeon racing is just as political. Because who dominates the skies, is suddenly up for debate.”

(GOVAN): In Tembisa, East of Johannesburg, Lepulana Motaloata has spent five years building a loft from scraps - and, with Lodumo’s help, has filled it with racers.
(Govan): “Your loft.. Tell me about the construction of it?”
(Lepulana Motaloata): “The construction, most of the construction is just collection from scrapyards… Scrap, scrap, scrap, scrap. And join everything together.”

(Govan): “Do you think you have a champion in there?”
(Lepulana Motaloata): “I think I might have a champion in there. I think so.”

(GOVAN): A single bird can cost thousands to rear and thousands more to race. That makes it more than a hobby for township fanciers who survive from one bag of feed to the next.

SLIDE: The Cost of Pigeon Racing in South Africa
Birds: R500 → R500,000+
Feed: ±R160 per bag
Medication & rings: R30 - R100+ each
Club fees: R2,000 – R5,000+ per year
Competitive budget: ±R80,000/year
Race entry: ±R14,000 per bird (Afrika Pro)

(Govan): “What’s holding you back from competing?”
(Lepulana Motaloata): “Ching ching, bra…”
(Govan): “Eish!”
(Lepulana Motaloata): “It’s very expensive to take care of these birds. When I tell someone I have racing pigeons they’re like ‘My man, you are rich.’ I say, ‘No, I’m not rich. It’s just the love.’”

GOVAN LINK: “Pigeon rearing has been happening in townships like these for generations, it’s nothing new. But the lofts are usually made out of anything that’s available. The real question is: how can these guys compete with established pigeon clubs, in races that are for big money, when the stakes are high?”

(GOVAN): Jimmy Shaban is among the new racers coming through Community Lofts.
(GOVAN): His Roodepoort loft, west of Joburg, already holds 40 birds.
(Jimmy Shaban): “I and my team are actually planning to, what is this, join the One Race Loft in Bloemfontein. Hopefully next year, we will be starting… for now we’re just focussing on breeding and selecting the best birds for actually competing to the races.”

(GOVAN): For Jimmy, Community Lofts offers the guidance to compete - but the cost of entry is steep.
(Govan): “How much is it to race in Bloemfontein?”
(Jimmy Shaban): “It’s, it’s R2000 per bird…”
(Govan): “And how many are you going to put in?”
(Jimmy Shaban): “We’re still planning with the team. Maybe a team of 20 birds, it will be decent.”
(Govan): “40 grand!”
(Jimmy Shaban): “Basically.”
(Govan): “Have you got that cash?”
(Jimmy Shaban): “Nah, we’re working on it, you know… We’re trying.”

(GOVAN): The sport has long shut newcomers out. Community Lofts is now opening doors.
(GOVAN): Young fanciers are pooling pigeons for next season, chasing trophies, and a place for township racers.
(Lodumo Nkala) “We would like to make pigeon racing a sport that’s accessible for everyone. No matter where you are, no matter how much money you have, what you can or can’t afford, it’s about making pigeon racing a sport that anyone with a dream can gain access to.”

SLIDE: The Cost of Pigeon Racing in South Africa Birds: R500 → R500,000+ Feed: ±R160 per bag Medication & rings: R30 - R100+ each Club fees: R2,000 – R5,000+ per year Competitive budget: ±R80,000/year Race entry: ±R14,000 per bird (Afrika Pro) (Govan): “What’s holding you back from competing?” (Lepulana Motaloata): “Ching ching, bra…” (Govan): “Eish!” (Lepulana Motaloata): “It’s very expensive to take care of these birds. When I tell someone I have racing pigeons they’re like ‘My man, you are rich.’ I say, ‘No, I’m not rich. It’s just the love.’” GOVAN LINK: “Pigeon rearing has been happening in townships like these for generations, it’s nothing new. But the lofts are usually made out of anything that’s available. The real question is: how can these guys compete with established pigeon clubs, in races that are for big money, when the stakes are high?” (GOVAN): Jimmy Shaban is among the new racers coming through Community Lofts. (GOVAN): His Roodepoort loft, west of Joburg, already holds 40 birds. (Jimmy Shaban): “I and my team are actually planning to, what is this, join the One Race Loft in Bloemfontein. Hopefully next year, we will be starting… for now we’re just focussing on breeding and selecting the best birds for actually competing to the races.” (GOVAN): For Jimmy, Community Lofts offers the guidance to compete - but the cost of entry is steep. (Govan): “How much is it to race in Bloemfontein?” (Jimmy Shaban): “It’s, it’s R2000 per bird…” (Govan): “And how many are you going to put in?” (Jimmy Shaban): “We’re still planning with the team. Maybe a team of 20 birds, it will be decent.” (Govan): “40 grand!” (Jimmy Shaban): “Basically.” (Govan): “Have you got that cash?” (Jimmy Shaban): “Nah, we’re working on it, you know… We’re trying.” (GOVAN): The sport has long shut newcomers out. Community Lofts is now opening doors. (GOVAN): Young fanciers are pooling pigeons for next season, chasing trophies, and a place for township racers. (Lodumo Nkala) “We would like to make pigeon racing a sport that’s accessible for everyone. No matter where you are, no matter how much money you have, what you can or can’t afford, it’s about making pigeon racing a sport that anyone with a dream can gain access to.”

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Pigeon racing isn’t a quirky side hustle - it’s a multimillion-rand obsession. • A single bird can sell for R5 million. • President Cyril Ramaphosa hosts the AfrikaPro Million Dollar Race on his Phala Phala estate. • Foreign syndicates bet millions. • And now? Township kids are clocking in faster birds than the elite - with none of the pedigree. But here’s the rub: Only a handful of South Africa’s 4,000 licensed fanciers are Black. Most clubs remain white-owned, white-run, and white-sanctioned. This isn’t a story about pigeons. It’s a story about power, access, and how legacy gets built - or stolen. While the elite race for prestige and profit, Black fanciers in the townships are often locked out - despite breeding birds that can fly just as far, just as fast. But a shift is in the air. And it smells like feathers and revolution.
metadata.Summary: It’s the most unlikely battlefield for race, class, and legacy in South Africa. Not Parliament. Not a protest. A pigeon coop. South Africa’s newest turf war is happening in the sky. In battered backyards and township rooftops, a new generation of Black pigeon fanciers is taking flight - and taking on an old guard that never saw them coming. Pigeon racing was once the playground of white suburban men: pedigree birds, pristine coops, and prize pots big enough to make a banker blush. Now? The game’s changing. They’re breeding champions in shacks. Clocking birds in car boots. Raising syndicates on social grants and second chances. And they’re not just racing pigeons - they’re upending a bloodline sport built on exclusion… one wingbeat at a time. Young, Black, and from the townships, they’re training world-class racers from the scrap heaps of apartheid’s leftovers. They don’t come from money. But they’ve got the hustle, the feathers, and the fire. And they’re not just racing pigeons - they’re rewriting the pecking order.
